Economy · Household data

Japanese households spent more yen—and bought less.

The average two-or-more-person household spent ¥310,975 in August. The price tag rose; the amount of consumption it represented fell. That gap is the clearest picture of Japan’s household squeeze.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 9, 2026 · 6 min read
August 2026 · two-or-more-person households¥310,975−3.1% after inflationSource: Statistics Bureau of Japan, released October 9

Japan’s newest household-spending report contains two statements that sound incompatible. Families spent an average of ¥310,975 in August, one percent more yen than a year earlier. Yet their spending fell 3.1%.

The missing phrase is “in real terms.” The first figure counts the money that left the household. The second adjusts for changing prices and asks how much that money could actually buy. When prices rise faster than expenditure, a family can hand over more cash while consuming less.

That is what the Statistics Bureau reported on October 9 for households with two or more people. The real year-on-year decline was the ninth in a row. July had been worse at minus 3.6%, and the seasonally adjusted August figure rose 0.1% from July, so the latest month is not a straight-line collapse. It is, however, a sustained loss of purchasing power.

The income line does not rescue the picture

Workers’ households received an average ¥616,704 in August. Nominal income rose 1.3% from a year earlier, but real income fell 0.9% under the Statistics Bureau’s preferred deflator excluding imputed rent, or 0.6% using the all-items consumer-price index. Pay packets became larger in yen and smaller in buying power.

This distinction explains why upbeat wage headlines can coexist with caution at restaurants, supermarkets and shops. A raise that trails the cost of living does not feel like additional room in a budget. It feels like a partial refund on higher prices.

The survey’s “average” is also not a recommended budget. It combines households with different sizes, incomes and spending obligations, then estimates the national pattern from a sample. Readers outside Japan should resist converting ¥310,975 into dollars and treating the result as a cost-of-living guide: exchange rates change, housing is handled differently across statistics, and a visitor’s basket is nothing like a resident family’s monthly basket.

9 monthsconsecutive real annual declines
+1.0%nominal spending change
+0.1%real monthly change, seasonally adjusted

Why one month can tell three stories

Year-on-year, month-on-month and nominal comparisons answer different questions. The 3.1% annual drop compares August 2026 with August 2025 after removing the effect of prices. It captures how far households are below the level of the same season a year ago. The 0.1% monthly rise adjusts for recurring seasonal patterns and suggests August was almost flat compared with July. The 1.0% nominal rise tells retailers and families how many yen changed hands.

Choosing only one can distort the story. “Spending increased” is technically true in nominal yen and from July after adjustment. “Spending declined” is also true in purchasing-power terms from a year earlier. The most useful reading is that households remain well below last year’s real consumption level, even though the latest monthly movement was no longer sharply negative.

A broader index points in the same direction

The government’s Consumption Trend Index, designed to supplement the household survey and include a broader view of consumption, put the real household-consumption index for all households at 97.7 in August on a 2025 base of 100. The macro total-consumption index was 100.8. Different measures cover different populations and use different methods, but neither turns the household story into a simple boom.

Online spending also cooled. The Survey of Household Economy reported that internet-shopping expenditure in August fell 1.4% in nominal terms from a year earlier, while the share of households shopping online slipped 2.2 percentage points to 54.9%. That is not evidence that Japanese consumers have abandoned e-commerce; more than half of surveyed households still used it. It does show that online channels are not automatically immune to the same budget pressure.

What to watch next

One release cannot identify every cause, and household averages conceal enormous differences by age, income, region and family structure. A retiree household exposed to food and utility prices experiences August differently from a working household paying school costs or rent. The figures also exclude one-person households from the headline two-or-more-person series.

The next useful tests are whether real wages turn positive, whether food inflation cools, and whether the year-on-year spending line breaks its nine-month decline. Japan’s policy debate often focuses on the yen, interest rates and headline wage agreements. The household survey translates those abstractions into the place where the economy becomes personal: the monthly sum a family can actually use.

¥310,975 looks like a precise answer. It is really the start of a question. If households are paying more but consuming less, how long can confidence recover before purchasing power does?
